intuition.title: Why use colloidal PbSe quantum dots
intuition.text: The authors motivate PbSe by its strong confinement and infrared transitions. They cite electron, hole and exciton Bohr radii of 23, 23 and 46 nm and describe a 3–8 nm colloidal size range. These are background/model scales, not particle-coordinate measurements. The source’s stated R/aB range is retained without recalculation or redefinition.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Introduction and reported confinement range

intuition.title: Temperature controls a series, not a supplied exact sample schedule
intuition.text: The paper varies injection and growth temperature within 80–150 °C and holds growth for 5–10 min. Higher temperatures produce larger dots, but it does not provide an exact temperature/time for each displayed size. The resulting record preserves that relationship without assigning endpoint temperatures to particular specimens.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Synthesis and size-control paragraphs

intuition.title: Single injection and purification
intuition.text: Lead acetate and oleic acid are heated in phenyl ether, cooled, mixed with the reported TOPSe stock, then injected into hot phenyl ether. The paper gives syringe capacity but no measured precursor volume. Repeated precipitation and centrifugation remove excess reagents; size-selective precipitation is stated to be unnecessary under favorable conditions, not mandatory as a separate unreported step.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Synthesis and analytical sample preparation

intuition.title: Structural evidence includes residual precursor
intuition.text: XRD is assigned to rock-salt PbSe and explicitly shows trace lead-oleate precursor peaks. STEM shows a close-packed ensemble and an approximately 7 nm lattice-resolved particle. The authors interpret its Pb-column image as a single crystal without internal defects, but no batch-wide defect fraction, shape distribution or atomic coordinate refinement is supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 1–2 and structure discussion

intuition.title: Optical transitions are not all uniquely assigned
intuition.text: The authors compare the approximately 8 nm absorption spectrum with Kang’s model. First and third transitions agree, while the second feature is not accounted for by the allowed-transition calculation. Parity-forbidden transitions and band anisotropy are discussed as alternatives; the article favors the former but states that no decisive assignment is made. Model arrows and bars are not additional measured materials.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and transition interpretation; references 15 and 22

intuition.title: High quantum yield does not prove a measured surface structure
intuition.text: The main reports room-temperature quantum yields of 12–81% without an inorganic semiconductor shell. Variation in surface reconstruction at reaction termination is suggested as an explanation, with comparison to earlier CdSe work. Actual surface reconstruction, ligand coverage and a per-size QY table are not measured.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 5 and quantum-yield discussion; reference 27

intuition.title: Long-lived emission and the later theoretical note
intuition.text: The 3 nm decay shown in Figure 6 has a 250 ns fitted time constant. The authors estimate an unscreened lowest-exciton transition-dipole radiative lifetime on the order of nanoseconds. They estimate that dielectric screening could increase it by as much as two orders of magnitude if bulk PbSe dielectric constants are assumed, while explicitly questioning whether bulk parameters apply to these nanocrystals. These are theoretical estimates, not additional measured lifetimes. Reference 28 adds a note that later calculations account for approximately 0.1 µs decay times; that cited full paper is not reviewed in this contribution, so the note remains source-attributed rather than independently confirmed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Figure 6, decay discussion and reference 28

intuition.title: Stokes shifts and application outlook remain qualified
intuition.text: Ensemble Stokes shifts of 40–90 meV are reported, but excitation well above the lowest exciton prevents direct identification with an intrinsic single-particle spectrum. Vibronic/non-Franck–Condon effects are proposed. Optoelectronics and fluorescence microscopy are motivations; no device performance or biological test is reported here.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 3–4, Abstract, Stokes-shift discussion and outlook; reference 23

general_background.title: Formation from dissolved precursors
general_background.summary: When dissolved species become supersaturated with respect to a solid, nucleation and growth can compete with continued precursor conversion. Mixing, complexation and solution chemistry can change that balance.
general_background.label: General background, not the authors' interpretation

reference.title: Mechanisms of Nucleation and Growth of Nanoparticles in Solution

general_background.title: From a metal precursor to reactive species
general_background.summary: A metal precursor supplies the metal, while its ligands and conversion chemistry influence how reactive species become available. Stronger or more persistent coordination can slow release of reactive metal species, while ligand exchange can open alternative conversion pathways.
general_background.label: General background, not the authors' interpretation

reference.title: Mechanisms of Nucleation and Growth of Nanoparticles in Solution

general_background.title: Conversion of a nonmetal precursor
general_background.summary: Chalcogen and pnictogen precursors can differ in how they release or transfer the element during a reaction. Bonding, coordination and the reaction medium can influence the activation or transfer steps that make an element available for growth.
general_background.label: General background, not the authors' interpretation
